lead: Most functions bend and twist. A linear map is the special kind that keeps the two operations of a vector space intact: add two vectors and then transform, and you get the same answer as transforming each one and adding afterwards. That single promise makes a linear map completely predictable — it is fixed once you know where the basis vectors go, which is why one matrix can store it. Rotations in a graphics engine, a weighted credit score, and the derivative of a polynomial all rest on this idea.
prereq: You need: vector spaces, subspaces and linear combinations from Unit 2, Vector Spaces.

blocks.text: A linear map is a function from one vector space to another that keeps both vector operations intact. Write it T: V → W, read "T from V to W". V is the domain, W is the codomain, and both are vector spaces over the same field F — in this unit usually R or C.
T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v)   and   T(cu) = c·T(u)
blocks.where: T: V → W is a function between vector spaces over the same field F; u, v are any vectors in V; c is any scalar in F. The first rule is additivity, the second is homogeneity (scaling). A map that satisfies both for all choices is called linear.

blocks.text: The two rules are really one. If T respects addition and scaling separately, it respects every linear combination: T(a u + b v) = a T(u) + b T(v). Checking that single line is enough, and most proofs use this combined form.

items: T(0) = 0. Put u = v = 0 in additivity: T(0) = T(0) + T(0), then subtract T(0) from both sides.
A linear map carries the zero vector of V to the zero vector of W. This is the fastest way to reject a candidate map.

A linear map sends each line through the origin to a line through the origin (or to {0}): T(tv) = t·T(v), so the image of the line spanned by v is the line spanned by T(v). The line may be stretched, shrunk or flattened, but it is never bent and it never moves off the origin.

sections.h3: Examples that pass, examples that fail

blocks.text: Six standard maps pass the test.

head: Map
Rule
Linear?
rows: T(x, y) = (x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ)

blocks.text: Every yes row passes for the same reason: the rule is built only from sums and scalar multiples. For the derivative, (p + q)′ = p′ + q′ and (cp)′ = c·p′ are the usual rules of calculus. Rotation is multiplication by a 2×2 matrix, so it inherits linearity from matrix multiplication. Scaling by c multiplies every length by |c| (a stretch when |c| > 1, a shrink when |c| < 1), keeps each direction when c > 0, reverses it when c < 0, and sends everything to 0 when c = 0.

The no rows fail in different ways. A constant shift moves the origin, so T(0) ≠ 0 — instant rejection. Squaring and coordinate products break scaling: doubling the input quadruples x² and doubles xy. Note that T(x) = x² does send 0 to 0, so the origin test can reject a map but can never prove linearity.

When domain and codomain are the same space, T: V → V is called a linear operator. Identity, scaling, rotation about the origin, projection onto a subspace, and the derivative on polynomials are all operators. Operators are the objects that get diagonalised later, in Unit 4, Eigenvalues, Diagonalization and Quadratic Forms.

blocks.where: S: U → V and T: V → W are linear maps; u is any vector in U; T ∘ S, read "T after S", is the composition, a map from U to W.

blocks.text: Composition keeps linearity in one line: (T ∘ S)(u + v) = T(S(u + v)) [definition of ∘] = T(S(u) + S(v)) [additivity of S] = T(S(u)) + T(S(v)) [additivity of T] = (T ∘ S)(u) + (T ∘ S)(v) [definition of ∘]. The scaling line is the same: (T ∘ S)(cu) = T(c·S(u)) = c·T(S(u)). Composition is not commutative in general: rotating then reflecting differs from reflecting then rotating. Sums and scalar multiples of linear maps are linear too, so the linear maps from V to W form a vector space of their own.

Two names, one idea. Some syllabi say linear transformation, others linear mapping; both mean the rule above. Once you choose bases, a linear map is stored as a matrix — that is matrix of a linear transformation and change of basis. Which inputs land on 0, and which outputs you can reach, comes next in kernel and range.

figure.caption: Two routes to the same result: add first then apply T, or apply T first then add. Additivity says the two must agree for every pair of inputs.

spec.title: Additivity check
spec.aria: A flow diagram sends u and v through addition then T, and separately through T then addition, meeting at a node that says the two results must be equal.

examples.question: Define T: R² → R² by T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y). (a) Show that T is linear. (b) Find T(1, 2). (c) Find T(e₁) and T(e₂), where e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1).
steps: Let u = (x, y) and v = (x′, y′) be any vectors in R², and let c be any real scalar.
Additivity: u + v = (x + x′, y + y′). Then T(u + v) = (2(x + x′) + (y + y′), (x + x′) − 3(y + y′)) = (2x + y + 2x′ + y′, x − 3y + x′ − 3y′) = T(u) + T(v).
Homogeneity: cu = (cx, cy). Then T(cu) = (2cx + cy, cx − 3cy) = c(2x + y, x − 3y) = c·T(u).
Both rules hold for every u, v and c, so T is linear. Origin check: T(0, 0) = (0, 0), as a linear map must give.

traps: T(0) = 0 is a quick rejection test, not a proof. T(x) = x² sends 0 to 0 and is still not linear.
A constant shift such as T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) is never linear, because T(0, 0) = (1, 0) ≠ (0, 0).
You must check both rules. Also test scaling with c = −1 and c = 1/2, not just whole numbers — maps that survive integers often fail on fractions or negatives.
The school "linear function" f(x) = mx + c is a linear map only when c = 0. The word is stricter here.
Domain and codomain must sit over the same field. If V is over C and W over R, the scalar i makes T(cu) = c·T(u) meaningless.

quiz.q: State the two rules that define a linear map T: V → W over a field F.
quiz.a: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) for all u, v in V; and T(cu) = c·T(u) for all u in V and all c in F.
A linear map T: V → V, that is, a linear map whose domain and codomain are the same vector space.

quiz.q: Explain why T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) is not linear.
quiz.a: T(0, 0) = (1, 0) ≠ (0, 0). A linear map must carry the zero vector to the zero vector, so this map fails immediately. Equivalently, T((0,0) + (0,0)) = (1, 0) but T(0,0) + T(0,0) = (2, 0).

quiz.q: T: R² → R² is given by T(x, y) = (3x − y, x + 2y). Find T(2, −1) and T(0, 0).
Let D: P₂ → P₂ send each polynomial to its derivative. Show D is linear using p(t) = t² + 3t and q(t) = 2t.
quiz.a: D(p) = 2t + 3 and D(q) = 2. p + q = t² + 5t, so D(p + q) = 2t + 5 = D(p) + D(q). For c = 4, D(4p) = D(4t² + 12t) = 8t + 12 = 4(2t + 3) = 4·D(p). Both rules hold, and the same argument works for all p, q, c.

quiz.q: Let T: R² → R be linear with T(1, 0) = 3 and T(0, 1) = −2. Find T(x, y) for general (x, y), then T(4, 5).
quiz.a: Any (x, y) = x(1, 0) + y(0, 1), so by linearity T(x, y) = x·T(1, 0) + y·T(0, 1) = 3x − 2y. Then T(4, 5) = 12 − 10 = 2. A linear map on R² is completely fixed by its two values on e₁ and e₂.

quiz.q: Is T(x, y) = (x + y, xy) linear? Justify with a single counterexample.
quiz.a: No. Take u = (1, 1) and v = (1, 1). T(u) = (2, 1) and T(u + v) = T(2, 2) = (4, 4), but T(u) + T(v) = (4, 2). Additivity fails, and scaling fails too: T(2, 2) = (4, 4) while 2·T(1, 1) = (4, 2).

beyond: Not for the exam. Linear maps are the workhorses of applied mathematics: a graphics card pushes every vertex through a rotation and scaling matrix, and a control system tracks a state through a linear operator at each time step. Machine learning uses x ↦ Wx + b, which is affine rather than linear — the bias b is exactly the constant shift that breaks the rule. Signal processing relies on the fact that the discrete Fourier transform is linear, so a sum of signals transforms to the sum of transformed signals. Search next for "affine map", "linear operator norm", and "matrix representation of a linear transformation".
